newsitem.title: AZERBAIJAN: Azerbaijan president asks NATO for security help.
newsitem.headline: Azerbaijan president asks NATO for security help.

text.p: Azeri President Haydar Aliyev asked NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana on Thursday for the alliance to do "everything possible" to help guarantee his oil-rich former Soviet republic's security.

"Azerbaijan is on the southeastern edge of Europe and we want NATO to do everything possible to guarantee our country's security," Aliyev told reporters in a joint briefing with Solana after the two held a two-hour meeting.

Solana is on the last leg of a tour of ex-Soviet states which has greatly irritated Russia. Moscow has alleged that NATO is pursuing a covert, anti-Russian policy in the region and the trip to Moldova, Armenia, Georgia and Azerbaijan, is an attempt to prevent former republics from integrating.

Clearly stung by the charges, Solana has defended his visit to the four republics, which like Russia are all participants in the Atlantic alliance's Partnership for Peace (PFP) programme that aims to forge closer ties between former Cold War foes.
Aliyev's warm embrace of NATO's role in what Moscow clearly regards as its strategic backyard would only seem to serve to further infuriate the former superpower.

Moslem Azerbaijan, although a member of the Commonwealth of Independent States, has had consistently troubled relations with Russia since the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991. It is the only Transcaucasian state with no Russian military bases.

Successive Azeri governments have accused Russia of backing its enemy, Christian Armenia, in an eight-year territorial dispute over the region of Nagorno-Karabakh as part of an effort to force it to give Moscow more of a role in lucrative Azeri Caspian Sea oil projects.
Aliyev said he also wanted the organisation to help bring an end to the conflict with Armenia, which claimed more than 15,000 lives before a ceasefire was declared almost three years ago.
Solana acknowledged Azerbaijan's geopolitical importance, saying that his talks with Aliyev had been "very useful" and that the alliance wanted to do much more to deepen ties.
"We consider Azerbaijan a serious and important partner. We are conscious of its political and economic importance," he said.
Azeri officals said that Solana and Aliyev had discussed a possible role for it in NATO peacekeeping missions.

Aliyev said his country of eight million had every intention of deepening ties and moving to a "new stage" in relations with the bloc through the PFP. "We think this program has great importance for us," he said.
Solana is scheduled to address the Azeri parliament on Friday before returning to NATO headquarters. None of the countries he visited are seeking alliance membership.

The war of words between Moscow and NATO comes as the alliance prepares to take in former Warsaw Pact member states from eastern and central Europe. Russia fiercely opposes NATO's eastward expansion as a threat to its own security. REUTER
